title: The US could soon make it easier to execute people with intellectual disabilities
summary:
A supreme court decision will determine whether the cruel, unconstitutional execution of people with intellectual disability becomes even more prevalent
The supreme court will soon rule on Hamm v Smith, an Alabama death penalty case that could significantly increase the number of people with intellectual disability who are executed. In this case, Alabama is fighting to execute a man named Joseph Smith. Smith’s five IQ scores – 72, 74, 74, 75 and 78 – all fall around the bottom fifth percentile of the population.
Based on these IQ tests, which measure learning, reasoning and problem-solving, and Smith’s adaptive behaviors, which include the social and practical skills that Smith uses to navigate everyday life, a federal court determined that Smith is intellectually disabled. Because the supreme court held in its landmark 2002 Atkins ruling that executing anyone with an intellectual disability violates the constitution, Alabama cannot execute Smith.
 Continue reading...

The father holds a mild physical disability certificate and receives a monthly low-income elderly subsidy of 4,664 NT dollars; the mother suffers long-term hip joint pain and had planned to rest but must now support the stall due to sudden family changes. The uncle also holds a mild physical disability certificate, receiving a monthly labor pension of 17,822 NT dollars, most of which pays for over 20,000 NT dollars of foreign caregiver fees monthly.

title: Conditions for vehicle license tax exemption for persons with disabilities relaxed further
summary: New Taipei City Tax Bureau announced that, to reduce the tax burden on caregivers of persons with disabilities and to fulfill the legislative purpose of Article 7, Section 1, Subparagraph 8 of the Vehicle License Tax Act, the Ministry of Finance issued an interpretation order on April 28, 2026, effective January 30, 2026. Persons with disabilities who hold a disability certificate and lack a driver's license due to their condition may have a vehicle owned by a relative within the second degree of kinship, whose registered address in the Motor Vehicle Information System matches the person's household address, and which is used by the person, be exempt from vehicle license tax, treating the residence address as the vehicle's tax location. The bureau reminded eligible vehicle owners to apply online via the Ministry of Finance tax portal with their disability certificate.
body:
New Taipei City Tax Bureau announced that, to reduce the tax burden on caregivers of persons with disabilities and to fulfill the legislative purpose of Article 7, Section 1, Subparagraph 8 of the Vehicle License Tax Act, the Ministry of Finance issued an interpretation order on April 28, 2026, effective January 30, 2026. Persons with disabilities who hold a disability certificate and lack a driver's license due to their condition may have a vehicle owned by a relative within the second degree of kinship, whose registered address in the Motor Vehicle Information System matches the person's household address, and which is used by the person, be exempt from vehicle license tax, treating the residence address as the vehicle's tax location. The bureau reminded eligible vehicle owners to apply online via the Ministry of Finance tax portal with their disability certificate.

summary:
Proposals also grant the health minister power to change disability support rules without state or territory approval. Here’s what you need to know

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Funding for some services within the national disability insurance scheme will be slashed – even in cases where participants could be left with a funding gap – as part of a sweeping proposal to drastically curb the scheme’s annual growth.
The proposed changes, revealed on Thursday, will also grant the health minister, Mark Butler, godlike powers to reduce overall funding for support categories, determine pricing guides and caps for services and support, and the ability to change NDIS rules without state and territory approval for the first 12 months.
